ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry Consultation — Nikola Tesla — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week sertraline tolerability and safety check, with psychiatry consultation

text.paragraph: Severe obsessive-compulsive symptoms (Y-BOCS 28) with good insight in a 45-year-old electrical engineer, with weight loss from food rituals and hand dermatitis from washing. Please confirm the diagnosis, review comorbidity, and advise on sertraline dosing, the length of the trial, and what to do if the response is partial. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within two weeks; no current suicidal ideation. [S]

list.item: Do you confirm obsessive-compulsive disorder, and is there a tic disorder, bipolar disorder, psychosis, obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, or an eating disorder to consider?
When and how fast should sertraline be raised, to what dose, and how long should the trial last before we judge it?
Is exposure and response prevention alone or combined with sertraline right for him?
What should we do if the response is partial at the maximum dose?
How should we handle his food rituals and weight loss, and his contamination fears during examinations?

text.paragraph: Mr. Tesla is seen at the request of Dr. Kovač-Holt, two weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg, which he tolerates with brief nausea. He describes contamination, symmetry, and number obsessions since childhood that have waxed and waned and worsened over the past six months under work pressure, with washing, counting, repeating, and calculating compulsions that take three to four hours a day. He resists them at a cost of rising anxiety and recognizes them as excessive. He has no motor or vocal tics, no period of elevated mood or reduced need for sleep with racing thoughts beyond his long-standing short sleep, no hallucinations or fixed false beliefs, no hoarding, and no concern about his appearance. His vivid imagery of designs is voluntary and recognized as his own. His perfectionism is confined to the rituals he finds distressing and does not otherwise rule his relationships. He does not fear weight gain or dislike his body shape; he skips meals because calculating them is exhausting. He has never harmed himself and has no suicidal thoughts. He drinks rarely and uses no drugs. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Nikola Tesla was born on 10 July 1856 in the village of Smiljan, in what is now Croatia, to Serbian parents; his father was an Orthodox priest. [D]

In his memoir My Inventions (1919) he wrote that in boyhood he suffered from "a peculiar affliction due to the appearance of images, often accompanied by strong flashes of light", pictures of things he had really seen, which caused him great discomfort and anxiety; at about twelve he first banished an image by wilful effort, but he never controlled the flashes, which grew stronger until he was about twenty-five. [D]

He wrote that he had a violent aversion to women's earrings, that the sight of a pearl would almost give him a fit, and that he would not touch the hair of other people; in 1919 he wrote that he was still "not insensible to some of these upsetting impulses". [D]

He wrote that he counted the steps in his walks and calculated the cubical contents of soup plates, coffee cups, and pieces of food, or his meal was unenjoyable, and that all repeated acts had to be divisible by three, and if he missed he felt impelled to do it all over again, even if it took hours. [D]
He wrote that from about seventeen he could visualize his inventions with the greatest facility and needed no models, drawings, or experiments. [D]
At seventeen he contracted cholera. [D]

In 1881 he moved to Budapest to help install a telephone exchange; there, in his own account, he suffered "the complete breakdown of the nerves", with extreme sensitivity to sound, light, and vibration, a pulse he described as ranging up to 260 beats, and twitching and tremors; a physician called his illness unique and incurable, and he recovered with a powerful desire to live and the help of a friend. [D]
In 1884 he went to New York; by 1901 he was building a tower and laboratory for wireless transmission at Wardenclyffe on Long Island. [D]
He claimed that his working hours at his first job in New York were from 10:30 in the morning until 5 the next morning, and even into old age he said he slept only two or three hours a night. [D]
A 2013 neurology review reads the experiences he described in his autobiography as including migraine auras, synesthesias, obsessions, and compulsions. [R]

The roster lists obsessive-compulsive disorder and probable autism spectrum features; no diagnosis was made in his lifetime, a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder is a later interpretation of his own accounts, and autism is speculative and is not diagnosed in this record. [R]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, severe, with good insight (F42.2). Confirmed: contamination, symmetry, and number obsessions with washing, counting, repeating, and calculating compulsions, severe by the Y-BOCS. No tic disorder, bipolar disorder, psychosis, hoarding, body dysmorphic disorder, or obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. The restricted eating is driven by the calculating ritual, not by fear of weight gain or of choking, so it is treated within the OCD plan rather than as a separate eating disorder. Depressive and anxiety symptoms are secondary. Acute suicide risk is low, and the safety plan is appropriate. [S]
Underweight from food rituals (R63.6). Needs regular meals now, with eating without calculating built into the exposure plan. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: The intake history, Y-BOCS 28 and today's 27, PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT-C, the laboratory results, the weight, and the collaborative safety plan. [S]

list.item: Combine weekly exposure and response prevention with sertraline, given severe symptoms. [S]

Keep sertraline at 50 mg for now; if the response is inadequate after four to six weeks, raise it in 50 mg steps every four to six weeks as side effects allow, up to 200 mg, with a check for side effects about two weeks after each increase. [S]
Judge the response only after eight to twelve weeks with at least four to six weeks at the top tolerated dose; a fall of 35 percent or more in the Y-BOCS is a response. [S]
Rate the Y-BOCS about every four to six weeks during titration; screen mood and suicide risk at each visit. [S]

If the response is still inadequate after an adequate trial at the highest tolerated dose, ask psychiatry about a switch to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmentation, with the monitoring each needs. [S]
Continue an effective dose for at least one to two years before any slow taper, with ERP booster sessions. [S]
Fixed mealtimes and dietitian support; examinations explained step by step, with hand hygiene offered, and no unplanned exposures outside therapy. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Kovač-Holt the same day; Mr. Tesla agrees with the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Primary care manages treatment with the clinic psychologist. Psychiatry is available for a further consultation on the criteria above. [S]
